The rest of the clause-joining family. Each one is a small phrase, and each one is wonderfully literal once you take it apart.

because → bili, or märr (ga):
Ŋarra rirrikthurruna bili barpuru ŋarra yätjkurru guya ḻuka → I'm sick because I ate a bad fish yesterday
Nhini dhiyala märr ga nhe ŋanya dhu yaka ŋoy-märrama → Sit here so that you won't annoy him

märr (ga) covers both because and so that, reason and purpose as one idea. (At Yirrkala they drop the ga entirely.)

until → yäna bili ga:
Ŋayi dhu marrtji yäna bili ga ŋayi ga marrtji räli Darwinlili → He'll go until he comes to Darwin

Take it apart: yäna (just) + bili (settled/complete) + ga (and). Until is literally just-until-it's-settled-and. The waiting is built from three words you already own.

before / and then → yurruna:
Yurruna nhe dhu ŋorra djorra' wukirri ŋarraku! → Before you lie down, write me a letter!
Ŋäthili ŋayi dhu ḻuka yurruna ŋayi ga gurrupan walalaŋgala → He'll eat first, before he gives it to them

And again the honest tense: before you WILL lie down. The lying-down is still future, so it's marked future. (There's ŋäthili again too, first, from way back.)

after → dhäŋuru ŋuliŋuru:
Dhäŋuru ŋuliŋuru ŋayi guya ḻukana ga ŋayi rirrikthurruna → After he ate the fish, he got sick

dhä is mouth/end, -ŋuru is the from suffix from Lesson 13. After = from the end of. The spatial suffix you learned for walking away from camp now walks you away from an EVENT. Space grammar becoming time grammar, that's not an accident, it's the whole worldview: time is a country you move through.

Even sweeter, the one-clause shortcut:
Dhäŋuru ŋathaŋuru ŋarra ŋanya dhu guwatjman → After the meal (from-the-end, from-the-food) I'll visit him

whether → wanha balaŋu:
Nhäŋu wanha balaŋu ŋayi rirrikthurruna → Look (and see) whether he is sick

wanha (where/which) + balaŋu (might): whether is literally which-maybe. Uncertainty located, like a place you haven't reached yet.

And the escape hatch: two clauses instead of one
The old fancy nominalisations can always be unfolded into plain clauses. I want to see the ship can be I want: I will see the ship. Ask her to cook can be Ask her: she will cook. The very last page of the old grammar book admits it: when in doubt, just say two simple things in a row. Fluency isn't maximal compression. It's knowing you're allowed to breathe.
